analysis.one_liner: Creates a government-run Medicare drug plan with negotiated prices and eliminates the Part D coverage gap.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in the Senate and referred to the Finance Committee, where it sat until the Congress ended without any vote.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have created a nationally available prescription drug plan run directly by Medicare, instead of the private insurance plans created under the 2003 Medicare drug law. It would require the Secretary of Health and Human Services to negotiate drug prices directly with pharmaceutical manufacturers — something the 2003 law expressly barred Medicare from doing. It would also lower out-of-pocket drug costs for everyone on Medicare Part D: the annual deductible would drop to match the Part B deductible, coinsurance would fall from 25% to 20%, and the 'coverage gap' (the 'donut hole' period when beneficiaries paid the full cost of their drugs) would be eliminated. The bill was referred to the Senate Finance Committee and never received a hearing, vote, or any further action before the 109th Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Medicare beneficiaries, especially those with high drug costs: the plan would give them a guaranteed, nationally available drug option with negotiated prices, a lower deductible, reduced coinsurance (20% instead of 25%), lower cost-sharing for low-income enrollees, and no donut-hole gap in coverage.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Seniors with high prescription drug costs

how_it_helps.text: Creates a Medicare-Guaranteed Prescription Drug Plan, available nationwide beginning in 2007, offering standard drug coverage with access to prices negotiated directly by Medicare [S2] [S3].

Overrides the 2003 law's 'non-interference' provision (section 1860D-11(i)) so Medicare could negotiate purchase prices with pharmaceutical manufacturers and use strategies similar to other federal drug purchasers, while encouraging affordable therapeutic equivalents when medically appropriate [S3].
Eliminates the Part D coverage gap by repealing the initial coverage limit, so beneficiaries no longer pay full drug cost in the middle of the year before catastrophic coverage kicks in [S2] [S3].

Cuts cost-sharing: the standard deductible becomes equal to the Part B deductible, coinsurance drops from 25% to 20%, low-income subsidies improve (15% to 10% and 25% to 20%), and no cost-sharing applies after the annual out-of-pocket threshold [S3].
Sets a uniform national premium for the new plan and sunsets the temporary 'fallback' and limited-risk plan provisions after 2006 [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name pharmaceutical manufacturers, whose revenue depends on Medicare paying negotiated market prices rather than prices set by private plans barred from bargaining; private Part D insurers and pharmacy benefit managers, who would compete with (and lose the fallback role to) a Medicare-run plan.
analysis.who_pays_short: Drug makers and private Part D insurers

drawbacks.text: Government price negotiation can reduce drug manufacturers' revenue, which critics argue would mean less investment in research and development of new medicines over time; the bill itself acknowledges this trade-off is real by requiring negotiation not to override medical necessity [S3].

Creating a competing Medicare-run plan and ending fallback and limited-risk plan authority after 2006 would disrupt the private Part D market built under the 2003 law, potentially displacing private plan choices beneficiaries had just enrolled in [S3].

The bill changes the financing mechanics of the drug benefit (including routing payments for the new plan through the Medicare prescription drug account) without an accompanying offset in the provided text, so the cost of deeper coverage would fall on Medicare spending or premiums [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For Medicare beneficiaries the gains are large and concrete: an end to the donut hole, a lower deductible, and reduced coinsurance, plus a plan whose whole purpose is securing lower drug prices through negotiation. The main costs fall on drug manufacturers and private plans, and the potential long-term cost is slower pharmaceutical innovation — a genuine trade-off, though one that other federal purchasers already accept. The bill is a straightforward attempt to redirect drug benefit spending away from intermediaries and toward lower prices for seniors.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in March 2006, sent to the Senate Finance Committee, and never got a hearing, a markup, or a vote before the Congress ended in January 2007.

narrative.text: Sen. Stabenow introduced the bill on March 1, 2006, with cosponsorship from Senate Democrats including Kennedy, Levin, Clinton, Akaka, Lautenberg, Boxer, and Dayton [S1] [S3] [S4].
The Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance the same day; that was the only chamber action recorded in the entire Congress [S1] [S5].
The bill carried only Democratic sponsorship — 9 Democratic cosponsors and no Republicans [S4].
No further action appears in the bill's action history through the end of the 109th Congress on January 3, 2007, meaning the bill died in committee [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name pharmaceutical manufacturers and private Part D insurers are better off because the bill never advanced: Medicare never gained negotiating authority, the private-plan structure of the 2003 drug benefit stayed intact, and seniors' drug costs were not reduced. Senate Republicans, who controlled the chamber and the Finance Committee, kept a clean record of never having to vote on it.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Drug makers and private drug plans

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever recorded, so the only visible split is sponsorship: 10 Democrats backed the bill (sponsor plus 9 cosponsors) and no Republican did [S4].

industries.note: The bill would let Medicare negotiate purchase prices directly with manufacturers, overriding the 2003 law's provision that barred Medicare from interfering with private-plan pricing. Manufacturers' Part D revenue depends on Medicare being unable to bargain, so their interest runs directly against lower prices for beneficiaries.

industries.industry: Private Part D insurers and pharmacy benefit managers
industries.note: A nationwide Medicare-run drug plan would compete with the private prescription drug plans at the center of the 2003 benefit design, and the bill would end the 'fallback' and limited-risk plan roles private insurers held after 2006. Their role as middlemen between Medicare and drug makers would shrink.
Lower negotiated acquisition prices would compress margins on Part D dispensing, but broader coverage (no donut hole) would mean fewer seniors skipping or rationing prescriptions, sustaining volume.
